newsitem.title: FRANCE: Poll - damaged Chirac limps to Denver summit.
newsitem.headline: Poll - damaged Chirac limps to Denver summit.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, his power gutted by a left-wing victory in a snap parliamentary election, limps to next week's Group of Seven summit in Denver almost a lame duck -- but not quite.

Chirac vaulted on to the world stage two years ago brimming with self-confidence and upstaged U.S. President Bill Clinton at a G7 summit in Halifax, Canada, shaming the West into action to end the war in Bosnia.

He hosted last year's summit of major industrial democracies in Lyon at the height of his power, pushing through a debt relief deal for poorer countries and a declaration of support for Russian President Boris Yeltsin's reform course.

Now Chirac is a mere shadow of his former self, doomed to share power in foreign affairs and defence with Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and to forfeit almost all say over economic and trade policy to the left-wing government.

France's poor economic performance, with sluggish growth, heavy taxes and the highest unemployment rate in the G7 at 12.8 percent, played a key role in the defeat of Chirac's centre-right coalition in a May 25-June 1 election.

Jospin, who has vowed to give jobs priority over austerity, has not yet decided whether to accompany Chirac to the G7 summit, as he plans to do at a European Union summit in Amsterdam next Monday and Tuesday.

But even if he doesn't, the Gaullist president who unleashed a furore by resuming nuclear tests in the South Pacific in 1995 will go to Denver as France's spokesman rather than its leader, flanked by Socialist foreign and finance ministers.

"Although Chirac brought it on himself, there is something tragic about his situation," a European diplomat said. "If he ploughs all that pent-up energy into foreign policy initiatives, we're in for a bumpy ride."

Chirac owes his misfortune to his own decision to dissolve parliament 10 months ahead of schedule, confident that his centre-right coalition, which had a huge majority of seats, would be re-elected. Instead, an alliance of Socialists, Communists and ecologist Greens won an upset victory.

Under the French constitution, the president signs treaties and guarantees their observance and is commander-in-chief of the armed forces, but the government determines and conducts the nation's policy, including on defence.

G7 leaders would be unwise to write Chirac off. He has the right to dissolve parliament again once the new legislature has run a year and could well win a renewed centre-right majority before his seven-year term expires in 2002.
In the meantime, he can speak for a broad consensus in France on most foreign policy issues.
There is no sign of a clash between Chirac, who has said he will be the guarantor of France's European commitments, and the Socialists on the conditions for a single European currency.

Jospin is holding up approval of a pact to limit the budget deficits of countries that join European economic and monetary union to demand a clause on coordinating member states' economic policies to promote growth.
During two previous periods of left-right "cohabitation", Chirac's wily Socialist predecessor, Francois Mitterrand, used G7 summits to assert his primacy in foreign affairs.
Mitterrand humiliated Chirac, then prime minister, when he insisted on attending a Tokyo G7 summit in 1986, posing protocol headaches for his Japanese hosts.
The French president will not be the only enfeebled leader at this year's G7 summit, set to become the G8 this year with the admission of Russia.

Veteran German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's sway at home has been sorely tested by deep budget troubles that have strained his coalition, and Russian President Boris Yeltsin's health remains uncertain following heart bypass surgery last year.
